questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You round a corner in a parking garage and see an adult slumped beside an idling car. Which action must you complete before kneeling next to the person?

answers.text: Move the person into the recovery position
Scan the scene for hazards such as traffic, fumes, or fire
Place an AED pad on the person before approaching
Begin chest compressions from where you are standing

explanations.a: Recovery position is for someone with normal breathing and pulse, not an opening assessment step.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 instructs rescuers to assess the surroundings for safety as the very first step so they do not become an additional victim.
explanations.c: AED pads can only be applied after pads are out and the rescuer is at the person's side.
explanations.d: Compressions cannot begin until the rescuer has reached a person they have judged safe to approach and confirmed unresponsive.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 1 lists examples of PPE that may be appropriate for a BLS rescuer depending on the situation. Which set of items best matches the manual's description?

answers.text: Only a stopwatch and clipboard for documentation
Medical gloves, eye protection, gowns or full-body suits, high-visibility clothing, safety footwear, and helmets
A defibrillator and medications kept in the rescuer's car
Only a single-use face shield kept in the rescuer's wallet

explanations.a: Documentation tools are not personal protective equipment.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 lists this combination of items — gloves, eye protection, gowns, high-visibility clothing, safety footwear, and helmets — as PPE that may be needed depending on the situation.
explanations.c: An AED and medications are emergency response equipment, not PPE.
explanations.d: A face shield alone is one barrier device; PPE is broader and varies by situation.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 1 directs BLS rescuers to consult specific organizations for additional information when a specific infectious disease is involved. Which organizations does the manual name?

answers.text: The local fire department and the National Park Service
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology
The Department of Transportation and the Federal Aviation Administration
Only the patient's primary care physician

explanations.a: These agencies do not provide infection-control guidance specific to BLS rescuers.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 names the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology (APIC) for additional infectious-disease information.
explanations.c: DOT and FAA are transportation agencies, not infection-control authorities.
explanations.d: A single physician is not an infection-control authority for BLS settings.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: After confirming the scene is safe, you reach an adult lying motionless on the floor. Which technique does AHA Part 2 specify for checking responsiveness in an adult?

answers.text: Pinch the cheek silently
Lift the eyelids to check pupil response
Tap the shoulders and shout, 'Hey! Are you OK? Are you OK?'
Sprinkle water on the face and watch for a flinch

explanations.a: Cheek-pinching is not the AHA-recommended responsiveness check.
explanations.b: Pupil checks are not part of the BLS responsiveness assessment.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 specifies tapping the shoulders and shouting, 'Hey! Are you OK? Are you OK?' for an adult or child.
explanations.d: Splashing water is not a recognized AHA responsiveness check and only delays activation.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: A daycare worker finds a motionless 4-month-old in a crib. After verifying the area is safe, where should they tap to check infant responsiveness?

answers.text: Both shoulders, the same as for an adult
The infant's heel
The forehead between the eyes
The abdomen near the navel

explanations.a: Shoulder tapping is for adults and children, not infants.
explanations.b: AHA Part 6 directs the rescuer to tap the infant's heel and shout to check responsiveness.
explanations.c: Forehead tapping is not the AHA-recommended infant assessment site.
explanations.d: Abdominal tapping is not part of any AHA responsiveness check.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You tap and shout at an adult on the floor and watch for any reaction. Which set of behaviors confirms the person is responsive?

answers.text: A heart rate over 100 with no chest movement
Cool extremities and pale skin
Movement, speech, blinking, or other reaction
Only a strong palpable pulse

explanations.a: Heart rate is a circulation finding, not a response to verbal and tactile stimulus.
explanations.b: Cool extremities and pale skin are signs of poor perfusion, not responsiveness.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 says someone responsive moves, speaks, blinks, or otherwise reacts when tapped and asked if they are OK.
explanations.d: A pulse alone does not establish responsiveness — many unresponsive cardiac patients still have a pulse.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You are alone in your home with an unresponsive adult who is not breathing normally, and your mobile phone is in your pocket. What is the AHA-recommended way to handle activation so you can begin care without delay?

answers.text: Run to a neighbor's house before any compressions
Wait until the next pause in CPR to call for help
Skip activation and continue CPR until someone else arrives
Dial the emergency number on your mobile phone, place it on speaker, and start CPR while talking to the dispatcher

explanations.a: Leaving the person to find a phone elsewhere delays compressions; modern guidance assumes mobile-phone use at the scene.
explanations.b: Activation must happen as early as possible — every minute lowers survival.
explanations.c: CPR alone without defibrillation rarely restores a pulse; EMS activation must occur as part of the early response.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2 supports using a mobile device with speaker mode so a lone rescuer can talk to dispatch while starting compressions.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: Two coworkers run over and ask how to help with an unresponsive adult on the office floor. As the lead rescuer, what is the most efficient way to use them?

answers.text: Have both stand back so they do not interfere
Send one to call for help and the other to retrieve the AED while you start compressions
Send both to call from separate phones for redundancy
Have one untrained bystander begin ventilations immediately

explanations.a: Trained or willing bystanders are valuable resources; sending them to act multiplies the speed of the response.
explanations.b: AHA Part 2 supports splitting tasks — one bystander activates EMS, one fetches the AED, and a third begins compressions — for the fastest path to defibrillation.
explanations.c: Two simultaneous emergency calls add no benefit and waste a person who could fetch the AED.
explanations.d: An untrained bystander should not begin ventilations; the higher-yield task for them is to bring the AED.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: A nurse finds an unresponsive patient in an inpatient room. Which method of activating the emergency response system does AHA Part 2 explicitly describe for the in-hospital setting?

answers.text: Wait for the next charting round to notify the team
Drive to the nearest fire station to summon help
Use a mobile device or an emergency response button to summon the rapid response team per institutional protocol
Send a written memo to the unit manager

explanations.a: Waiting for a charting round delays the rapid response team and is incompatible with cardiac arrest timing.
explanations.b: Hospitals have internal emergency response systems; rescuers do not leave the unit for help.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 describes activating in-hospital help by mobile device or an emergency response button, following the institution's protocol.
explanations.d: A written memo is not real-time activation and would not summon the rapid response team in time.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: How long does AHA BLS specify for a simultaneous check of breathing and pulse on an unresponsive adult?

answers.text: At least 5 but no more than 10 seconds
At least 30 seconds
Exactly 60 seconds
At least 20 seconds, repeated three times

explanations.a: AHA Parts 2 and 6 specify checking breathing and pulse simultaneously for at least 5 but no more than 10 seconds.
explanations.b: 30 seconds pushes the start of compressions far past the recommended window.
explanations.c: 60 seconds is far longer than current guidance and creates unacceptable delay before CPR.
explanations.d: Repeating a 20-second check three times produces a 60-second delay, contrary to AHA timing.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: While simultaneously checking the pulse on an unresponsive adult, what does AHA Part 2 instruct the rescuer to do to assess breathing in the same window?

answers.text: Place an ear over the nose and listen for sound only
Pinch the nostrils and watch for the abdomen to rise
Auscultate the lungs with a stethoscope from front and back
Scan the person's chest for at least 5 but no more than 10 seconds to see if it rises

explanations.a: Listening with the ear alone misses many breaths; AHA specifies scanning the chest visually.
explanations.b: Pinching nostrils is part of giving rescue breaths, not checking breathing.
explanations.c: Stethoscope auscultation is a clinical exam technique, not the AHA BLS breathing-check method.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2 instructs rescuers to scan the chest for at least 5 but no more than 10 seconds for visible rise and fall.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: After 8 seconds of a simultaneous breathing-and-pulse check on an unresponsive adult, you have not definitely felt a pulse and the chest is motionless. What does AHA guidance direct you to do next?

answers.text: Continue checking the pulse for another full minute
Wait until breathing changes before deciding
Reposition the person and check again from the beginning
Start high-quality CPR beginning with chest compressions

explanations.a: Extending the pulse check past 10 seconds is contrary to AHA guidance and only delays compressions.
explanations.b: Waiting for breathing changes is not part of the algorithm; cardiac arrest has already been recognized.
explanations.c: Restarting the check delays CPR; once cardiac arrest is recognized, compressions begin without further re-checking.
explanations.d: If a pulse is not definitely felt within 10 seconds and the person is not breathing normally, AHA directs the rescuer to start high-quality CPR with compressions.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: An adult collapses in front of you. You note slow, irregular gasping sounds with long pauses between them. According to the AHA Provider Manual, what do these gasps most likely represent?

answers.text: A reliable indicator that the person is recovering
Normal sleep breathing that requires no intervention
A sign of cardiac arrest requiring CPR
A sign the person needs only oxygen by nasal cannula

explanations.a: Agonal gasping is a sign of arrest, not recovery, and rescuers who mistake it for recovery delay lifesaving care.
explanations.b: Sleep breathing is regular and quiet, not the slow irregular gasps with long pauses described in agonal breathing.
explanations.c: AHA explicitly states agonal gasps are common in the first few minutes of cardiac arrest and are a sign that CPR is needed.
explanations.d: Supplemental oxygen alone does not address pulselessness and would skip the needed compressions.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: A trainee asks how agonal breathing actually sounds and looks so they can recognize it in the field. Which description matches AHA's characterization of agonal gasps?

answers.text: Steady, even breaths at a rate of 12 to 20 per minute
Loud, continuous wheezing with each breath
Silent, completely absent chest movement
Gasps, snorts, snores, or groans that may be forceful or weak with time passing between them

explanations.a: Steady even breaths describe normal breathing, not agonal gasping.
explanations.b: Continuous wheezing suggests bronchospasm rather than the irregular gasps of an arrest.
explanations.c: Completely absent breathing is total apnea, which differs from the irregular gasps that define agonal breathing.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 describes agonal breathing as gasps, snorts, snores, or groans that may be forceful or weak with pauses between them.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: respiratory arrest with pulse give breaths
questions.text: An adult is unresponsive and has only occasional gasps, but you do feel a definite, regular pulse during your simultaneous check. According to AHA guidance, what is the appropriate next action?

answers.text: Provide rescue breaths or ventilation without chest compressions and reassess
Start chest compressions immediately because gasping equals arrest in all cases
Wait silently for the gasping to stop before doing anything
Place the person in the recovery position and walk away

explanations.a: AHA guidance for an unresponsive person who is gasping but has a pulse is to provide breaths or ventilation without compressions and reassess.
explanations.b: Compressions are reserved for pulselessness; this person has a definite pulse.
explanations.c: Doing nothing while the person is in respiratory failure invites progression to cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: Recovery position is for someone with normal breathing; gasping with poor ventilation requires active rescue breaths.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You are checking a pulse on an unresponsive adult during the simultaneous breathing-and-pulse assessment. Which artery does AHA BLS direct you to palpate?

answers.text: The brachial artery in the upper arm
The carotid artery in the neck
The dorsalis pedis artery in the foot
The radial artery at the wrist

explanations.a: The brachial artery is the recommended pulse-check site for infants, not adults.
explanations.b: AHA BLS uses the carotid artery in the neck for pulse checks in adults and children.
explanations.c: The dorsalis pedis is not used for cardiac arrest pulse checks; it is unreliable in low-flow states.
explanations.d: The radial pulse can be hard to feel during low cardiac output and is not the BLS-specified site.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You are assessing an unresponsive 6-month-old infant. Which pulse check site does AHA Part 6 specifically direct you to use?

answers.text: The carotid pulse in the neck
The femoral artery only
The dorsalis pedis on the foot
The brachial artery on the inside of the upper arm, midway between the elbow and shoulder

explanations.a: Carotid pulse is used for adults and children, not infants, where the short neck and small landmarks make it unreliable.
explanations.b: The femoral artery is an option for a child but is not the AHA-specified primary site for infants.
explanations.c: Dorsalis pedis is not used in BLS pulse checks at any age.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs rescuers to feel the brachial pulse on the inside of the upper arm, midway between the elbow and shoulder, for an infant.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You are assessing pulse on a 4-year-old in cardiac arrest and the carotid landmark is hard to identify because of body habitus. Which alternative pulse site does AHA Part 6 explicitly allow for a child?

answers.text: The temporal artery on the forehead
The radial artery palpated at the wrist
The femoral artery in the inner thigh
The popliteal artery behind the knee

explanations.a: The temporal artery is not a BLS pulse-check site.
explanations.b: Radial pulse is unreliable in low-flow arrest states and is not listed as a BLS pulse-check site.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 names the femoral artery in the inner thigh — midway between the hip bone and pubic bone — as an alternative to the carotid for children.
explanations.d: The popliteal site is not described in BLS pulse-check guidance.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: An instructor asks the class to define perfusion as the term is used in AHA pediatric BLS. Which statement matches the manual's definition?

answers.text: The flow of oxygenated blood from the heart through the arteries to the body's tissues
The amount of air the lungs hold during inspiration
The electrical activity recorded on an ECG
The percent of oxygen bound to hemoglobin in venous blood

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 defines perfusion as the flow of oxygenated blood from the heart through the arteries to the body's tissues.
explanations.b: Lung volume describes ventilation, not perfusion.
explanations.c: ECG activity is electrical conduction, not blood flow itself.
explanations.d: Venous oxygen saturation measures oxygen delivery but is not the AHA definition of perfusion.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You are assessing a child whose pulse is borderline. Which combination of findings does AHA Part 6 list as signs of poor perfusion that should guide your next decision?

answers.text: Warm pink extremities and a strong bounding pulse
A respiratory rate of 14 per minute and clear lung sounds
Cool extremities, declining mental status, weak pulses, and pallor with mottling or cyanosis
Brisk capillary refill and an alert, oriented mental state

explanations.a: Warm pink skin with strong pulses indicates good perfusion, not poor perfusion.
explanations.b: A normal respiratory rate with clear lung sounds is reassuring rather than a sign of poor perfusion.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 lists cool extremities, declining mental status, weak pulses, and pale or mottled skin progressing to cyanosis as signs of poor perfusion.
explanations.d: Brisk capillary refill with an alert state indicates intact perfusion.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: HR less than 60 poor perfusion start CPR
questions.text: You are providing breaths to a child in respiratory failure when reassessment shows a heart rate of 50 per minute with cool, mottled extremities and continued declining responsiveness despite oxygenation and ventilation. What does the AHA pediatric BLS algorithm direct you to do next?

answers.text: Continue ventilations only and do not start chest compressions
Wait two more minutes before any change in care
Begin CPR with chest compressions and ventilations
Stop all care and reassess after the parents arrive

explanations.a: Ventilations alone are insufficient when heart rate is under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation.
explanations.b: Delaying intervention worsens outcome; the algorithm calls for an immediate change in care.
explanations.c: AHA Part 6 directs the rescuer to start CPR when a child's heart rate is under 60 with signs of poor perfusion despite oxygenation and ventilation.
explanations.d: Stopping care to wait for family is never the correct algorithm action during a deteriorating pediatric resuscitation.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: witnessed child collapse activate get AED return
questions.text: You are alone with a child you saw suddenly collapse, and no mobile device is available. According to AHA pediatric BLS, what is the recommended sequence?

answers.text: Stay at the child's side and wait for someone to find you
Provide 30 minutes of CPR before any activation
Continue checking responsiveness every minute and do nothing else
Leave the child to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR

explanations.a: Doing nothing while waiting wastes minutes during which the brain is being deprived of oxygen.
explanations.b: An indefinite delay before activation contradicts the witnessed-collapse rule and lowers survival.
explanations.c: Repeated responsiveness checks without action do not address cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: AHA Part 6 directs a lone rescuer who witnessed a child's sudden collapse to leave to activate EMS and get an AED, then return to perform CPR.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: You are alone with an unresponsive infant whose collapse you did not witness, and you have no mobile device. Which sequence does AHA Part 6 recommend?

answers.text: Perform 5 cycles, or about 2 minutes, of CPR first, then leave to activate EMS and get an AED
Leave immediately to call for help before any CPR
Provide breaths only and do not perform compressions
Wait for the parents before starting any care

explanations.a: AHA Part 6 directs the lone rescuer at an unwitnessed infant or child collapse without a mobile device to perform 5 cycles, or about 2 minutes, of CPR before leaving to activate EMS and get an AED.
explanations.b: Leaving an unwitnessed pediatric arrest victim before any CPR omits the most important early intervention for a respiratory cause.
explanations.c: Breaths-only ignores the compression component required for both respiratory and cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: Waiting for parents wastes minutes during which oxygen delivery to the brain is failing.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes the Team Leader's responsibilities during a high-performance resuscitation. Which set of duties matches?

answers.text: Performs all chest compressions personally throughout the resuscitation
Assigns roles to team members, oversees performance, makes treatment decisions, and serves as a coach and mentor
Documents the events from outside the room only
Operates the AED while a coworker assigns all other roles

explanations.a: The Team Leader oversees the entire resuscitation rather than performing one specific role like compressions throughout.
explanations.b: AHA Part 5 lists the Team Leader's duties as assigning roles, overseeing performance, making treatment decisions, and serving as a coach and mentor.
explanations.c: Documentation from outside the room is not the Team Leader role; the Team Leader is at the resuscitation.
explanations.d: Role assignment is the Team Leader's responsibility, not the AED operator's.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 explains how the Compressor role rotates during a sustained resuscitation. What is the typical rotation cadence?

answers.text: Every 30 seconds in the middle of a cycle
Between cycles every 2 minutes for seamless transitions
Only when the rescuer asks for relief
After every breath delivered

explanations.a: Switching every 30 seconds increases pause frequency and lowers CCF.
explanations.b: AHA Part 5 says compressors rotate between cycles every 2 minutes for seamless transitions, often timed with rhythm checks or AED analyses.
explanations.c: Waiting until the rescuer asks may produce fatigue-related quality drops before the swap.
explanations.d: Switching after every breath produces dozens of unnecessary pauses per minute.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes the Monitor/Defibrillator role on a high-performance team. Which set of responsibilities matches?

answers.text: Charts every team conversation in real time
Performs only ventilations during the resuscitation
Manages family presence outside the room
Brings and operates the AED, monitor, or defibrillator and may also act as the CPR Coach if designated

explanations.a: Charting conversations is not the AHA-described Monitor/Defibrillator role.
explanations.b: Ventilations are a separate role assignment on the high-performance team.
explanations.c: Family-presence management is handled by other team members or institutional liaisons.
explanations.d: AHA Part 5 says the Monitor/Defibrillator brings and operates the AED, monitor, or defibrillator and may act as the CPR Coach if designated.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: team owns code triangle no one leaves
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes a principle about how team members behave during a high-performance resuscitation. Which statement matches?

answers.text: The team owns the code; no team member leaves the triangle except to rotate compressors or to protect their own safety
Any team member can leave the resuscitation at any time without coordination
Only the Team Leader stays; everyone else rotates in and out freely
Team members should leave the room every 5 minutes to rest

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 says the team owns the code and no team member leaves the triangle except to rotate compressors or to protect their own safety.
explanations.b: Free movement breaks team cohesion and degrades CPR quality.
explanations.c: Multiple team members are essential to high-performance care; none rotate freely without role coordination.
explanations.d: Routine 5-minute rest breaks would interrupt continuous high-quality CPR.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes closed-loop communication as a technique that prevents misunderstandings during a resuscitation. Which sequence captures the technique?

answers.text: The sender gives the message, the receiver repeats it back, and the sender confirms it was heard correctly
The sender gives the message and assumes it was understood
The sender writes the message on a whiteboard for later review
The receiver waits silently until the next pause to ask for clarification

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 says closed-loop communication consists of the sender giving the message, the receiver repeating it back, and the sender confirming it was heard correctly.
explanations.b: Assuming a message was understood is exactly what closed-loop communication is designed to prevent.
explanations.c: Whiteboards are documentation tools and are not part of the closed-loop verbal exchange.
explanations.d: Silent waiting until later breaks the loop and risks errors during the active resuscitation.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: team leader call by name eye contact
questions.text: AHA Part 5 lists specific Team Leader behaviors that support closed-loop communication. Which behavior matches?

answers.text: Whisper instructions to one team member at a time
Issue instructions only by writing on a chart
Avoid eye contact to maintain authority
Call each team member by name and make eye contact when giving an instruction

explanations.a: Whispering reduces audibility and prevents the rest of the team from hearing the instruction.
explanations.b: Written instructions during an active code are too slow for time-critical actions.
explanations.c: Avoiding eye contact undermines the explicit handoff that closed-loop communication relies on.
explanations.d: AHA Part 5 directs the Team Leader to call each team member by name and make eye contact when giving an instruction, and to wait until the team member confirms understanding before assigning more.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 explains how to handle a situation in which a team member appears mistaken about a drug, dose, or intervention. Which approach does the manual recommend?

answers.text: Intervene tactfully and constructively to point out the error
Stay silent because intervention damages morale
Wait until after the resuscitation ends and then file a formal complaint
Shout the correction across the room to ensure attention

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 says when intervening, it is important to do so in a tactful and constructive way, especially when someone is mistaken about a drug, dose, or intervention.
explanations.b: Staying silent allows a treatment error to occur — the opposite of the AHA recommendation.
explanations.c: Waiting until after the code permits the error to harm the patient and is not the AHA approach.
explanations.d: Shouting damages team dynamics and is not the constructive approach AHA describes.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: CPR Coach feedback depth rate recoil
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes the CPR Coach's role in supporting high-quality CPR. Which set of metrics does the coach specifically use the feedback device data to address?

answers.text: Battery level of the AED only
Patient skin color and pupil size
Compression depth, rate, and chest recoil
Bystander head count and ambient noise

explanations.a: Battery level is a maintenance check, not a real-time CPR quality metric.
explanations.b: Skin color and pupils are clinical observations, not the metrics the feedback device monitors.
explanations.c: AHA Part 5 says the CPR Coach gives feedback specifically about compression depth, rate, and chest recoil because visual assessment of CPR quality is often inaccurate.
explanations.d: Bystander count and noise are situational and not part of CPR quality feedback.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes how the CPR Coach should communicate targets to the Compressor. Which approach matches?

answers.text: Tell the Compressor to stay 'somewhere in the recommended range'
State specific midrange targets, such as a rate of 110 per minute rather than 100 to 120
Avoid giving any numerical targets to prevent distraction
Give targets only after the resuscitation has ended

explanations.a: Vague guidance does not help the Compressor stay precisely on target.
explanations.b: AHA Part 5 says the CPR Coach states specific midrange targets so that compressions and ventilation are within the recommended range — for example, telling the Compressor to compress at 110 per minute rather than between 100 and 120.
explanations.c: Numerical targets are exactly what the CPR Coach is supposed to provide.
explanations.d: Coaching after the resuscitation ends is debriefing, not coaching during the code.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: I am the CPR Coach announcement coordinate
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes how the CPR Coach should begin coordinating CPR once the patient is identified as having no pulse. Which action matches?

answers.text: Wait silently until the Team Leader calls on them
Begin compressions personally while the team watches
Move all team members away from the patient first
State 'I am the CPR Coach' and tell rescuers to begin chest compressions, then adjust the environment as needed

explanations.a: Silently waiting wastes time when CPR needs to start immediately.
explanations.b: The Compressor performs compressions; the CPR Coach coordinates and gives feedback.
explanations.c: Moving team members away is the opposite of coordination.
explanations.d: AHA Part 5 says as soon as a patient is identified as having no pulse, the CPR Coach says, 'I am the CPR Coach,' tells rescuers to begin compressions, and adjusts the environment to facilitate high-quality CPR.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 describes the purpose of debriefing after a resuscitation event. Which set of goals best matches the manual's description?

answers.text: Evaluate process and CPR performance, reflect on team dynamics, provide education for quality improvement, and process emotions
Assign blame to the team member responsible for any errors
Document only the time of arrest for the medical record
Conduct a financial review of the resources used

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 says debriefing is an opportunity for evaluating process and CPR performance, reflecting on team dynamics, providing education for quality improvement, and processing emotions after a stressful event.
explanations.b: Blame assignment is not the AHA-described purpose; debriefing is about learning, not punishment.
explanations.c: Documentation is a separate task from debriefing.
explanations.d: Financial review is not the AHA-described debriefing purpose.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.keyword: CCF formula compression time over total
questions.text: AHA Part 5 provides a formula for calculating chest compression fraction manually after a resuscitation. Which formula matches?

answers.text: CCF = total code time divided by actual chest compression time
CCF = number of compressions divided by number of breaths
CCF = actual chest compression time divided by total code time
CCF = number of shocks divided by total code time

explanations.a: Total time over compression time inverts the ratio and produces a value greater than 1.
explanations.b: The compression-to-breath ratio describes the CPR cycle, not chest compression fraction.
explanations.c: AHA Part 5 says CCF equals actual chest compression time divided by total code time.
explanations.d: Shocks per total time is not how CCF is calculated.

questions.name: Assessment and High-Performance Teams
questions.text: AHA Part 5 cites research on the relationship between chest compression fraction and survival. Which relationship does the manual report?

answers.text: A 10 percent increase in CCF is roughly equal to an 11 percent increase in survival
A 50 percent increase in CCF correlates with a 1 percent increase in survival
CCF has no measurable impact on survival
CCF should be kept below 50 percent to allow for analysis

explanations.a: AHA Part 5 reports that research shows a 10 percent increase in CCF is roughly equal to an 11 percent increase in survival.
explanations.b: The relationship is roughly 1:1, not 50:1.
explanations.c: CCF has a strong, documented relationship with survival from cardiac arrest.
explanations.d: Keeping CCF intentionally low contradicts AHA guidance and lowers survival.
